# Dark-triplet-induced instability and eﬃciency roll-oﬀin blue phosphorescent organic light-emitting devices

(Received 10 February 2025; revised 25 June 2025; accepted 7 January 2026; published 17 February 2026)

The relative instability of high-eﬃciency blue phosphorescent organic light-emitting devices (OLEDs) is an important and longstanding challenge. Conventional models of degradation emphasize the dynamics of emissive triplet excitons on phosphorescent molecules, neglecting the potential role of nonemissive, “dark,” triplet excitons on host and charge blocking molecules. Bright and dark triplet dynamics are probed in situ using surface plasmon polariton-coupled modulation and magnetic exciton annihilation modulation, respectively. It is observed that dark triplet excitons dominate both the instability and eﬃciency roll-oﬀof a high-performance blue phosphorescent OLED. Dissociating dark triplets both improves device stability and reduces eﬃciency losses at high brightness by a factor of 2. The combined beneﬁt to stability of Purcell engineering and dark triplet management is a factor of 3.5. The results demonstrate that dark triplet excitons reduce the potential beneﬁt of Purcell engineering, emphasizing the importance of in-situ characterization and control of dark triplets to realize the goal of stable blue phosphorescent OLEDs.

## I. INTRODUCTION

High-eﬃciency organic light-emitting devices (OLEDs) harness energy stored in spin-1 “triplet” excited states, or excitons. Triplets are typically long-lived dark states, with spin-disallowed emission. To harness their energy for electroluminescence, phosphorescent OLEDs use heavy metals such as Pt or Ir to mix triplet states with spin- 0 “singlets” [1–6], allowing light emission directly from the triplet [7]. Exciton radiative lifetimes in such devices are typically on the order of microseconds [1], roughly 1000× longer than the radiative lifetimes in a typical ﬂuorescent OLED, with a corresponding increase in the energy density stored within the device. Long exciton lifetimes also exacerbate the probability of collisions with another excited state or charge, known as triplet-triplet annihilation (TTA) and triplet-polaron annihilation (TPA),

Triplet annihilation in blue OLEDs generates high-energy states carrying up to 6 eV—large enough to break intramolecular bonds—and has been identiﬁed as an important contributor to OLED instability [12]. Phosphorescent technologies are presently used to generate green and red colors in OLED displays. But realizing a stable high-eﬃciency blue OLED remains an outstanding problem. One proposed solution is “Purcell enhancement,” which increases the rate of light emission to better compete with triplet annihilation processes, thereby enhancing stability and minimizing eﬃciency losses [13]. Indeed, signiﬁcantly improved stability has been realized by reducing phosphorescent lifetimes in an optical study by Ha et al. [13] as well as prior work on OLEDs [14,15]. OLED studies, however, have shown that changes in the lifetime of emissive “bright” triplets do not simply correlate with the observed eﬃciency “roll-oﬀ” [9], as might be expected for phenomena dependent on the annihilation of bright triplets. Indeed, studies of OLED eﬃciency ascribe a dominant role to “dark” losses that are expected to be immune to Purcell engineering because they do not involve bright triplets [9]. In this work, we investigate “dark” processes in blue phosphorescent OLEDs and their role in device instability. We show that conventional models of blue phosphorescent

OLEDs are incomplete in their neglect of long-lived, “dark” triplets that can accumulate on host and charge blocking materials. We demonstrate experimental techniques to identify dark triplets within operating OLEDs, and we show that unless they are deliberately managed, dark triplets can dominate the dynamics of degradation and eﬃciency roll-oﬀ. In particular, we analyze exciplex hosts, which are observed to improve the performance of some blue phosphorescent devices [6]. Although the role of exciplex hosts is sometimes described as improving “charge balance,” we ﬁnd that the reduction of bright triplet quenching by more evenly-distributed charges cannot explain the full device impact of exciplex hosts. Instead, we determine that exciplex hosts quench dark triplets, approximately doubling the potential beneﬁt of Purcell engineering of bright triplet states. The combination of Purcell engineering and the use of exciplex hosts that quench dark triplets is observed to improve the stability of blue OLEDs by a factor of ×3.5.

## II. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN

## A. Exciton dynamics

A model of exciton dynamics in phosphorescent OLEDs is shown in Fig. 1(a). In the ideal case, injected charge either recombines directly on phosphorescent molecules or generates excitons in the host that quickly transfer to phosphorescent molecules, thereby generating emissive triplet excitons and ultimately producing light. Annihilation reactions involving bright triplets compete with light emission, causing degradation and eﬃciency losses [11,13–15]. To quantify how the rate of annihilation reactions is impacted

by changes in the bright triplet lifetime, we seek experimental isolation of the latter. As schematically shown in Fig. 1(b), bright triplet lifetimes can eﬃciently be modulated by near-ﬁeld coupling to polaritonic acceptor modes at nearby dielectric-metal interfaces [13]. Thus, OLED cathodes with common electrical properties but externally varied optical characteristics [16,17] can be used to implement surface plasmon polariton modulation (SPPM) of the bright triplet lifetime to determine its impact on device stability and eﬃciency roll-oﬀ. As discussed below, conventional models of OLED degradation typically neglect excited states on host or charge blocking molecules because such triplet states are expected to be rapidly harvested by the phosphor [7,8]. These excitons are nonemissive, “dark” states and diﬃ- cult to probe due to their ineﬃcient phosphorescent decay. To detect the presence of dark excitons, we note that the diﬀering properties of bright and dark triplet excitons are related to the splitting of the triplet sublevels at zero magnetic ﬁeld. Dark triplets have a small zero ﬁeld splitting (ZFS) of ∼10 μeV due to the absence of appreciable spin-orbit coupling. Strong spin-orbit coupling on phosphors, however, yields much larger ZFS of ∼1–100 meV [18]. Thus, moderate magnetic ﬁelds (B < 0.4 T) modulate TPA and TTA processes that only involve dark triplets, while the dynamics of bright triplets are unaﬀected. Consequently, we employ magnetic exciton annihilation modulation (MEAM) to probe for the presence of dark triplets, allowing us to nondestructively obtain spectroscopic signatures of annihilation events involving dark triplet states. In Fig. 1(c), we show representative magnetic ﬁeld dependencies of TPA and TTA following Merriﬁeld theory [19].

If triplets interact in a TTA process, the combination of two triplets has nine possible spin states: one singlet, three triplets, and ﬁve quintets. The quintets can mix with the singlet because these species have the same symmetry under exchange. An applied magnetic ﬁeld alters the rate of TTA by varying the distribution of singlet character in the mixed singlet-quintet states. The pure quintet is energetically inaccessible; thus the singlet character controls the rate of TTA. Note that the triplet TT pairs are unaffected by the ﬁeld because they do not mix with singlets or quintets. At zero ﬁeld, three states have some singlet character; at high ﬁeld, two states have singlet character [19]. If we assume that the nine TT pairs are populated randomly, then the overall trend is that the applied magnetic ﬁeld slows down the TTA process. At intermediate ﬁelds, however, there can be degeneracies, which increase the number of states with some singlet character [19]. This increases the TTA rate at low ﬁelds and yields a zero crossing in the overall TTA characteristic. The zero crossing is the distinctive signature of a TTA process. The interaction of triplets and charges is simpler. The initial system has total spin of 3/2 and consists of a

quartet and a doublet [20]. After annihilation the total spin is 1/2. The magnetic ﬁeld systematically decreases the number of initial states with doublet character, reducing the rate of triplet-charge annihilation. Thus, triplet-charge annihilation slows monotonically with applied magnetic ﬁeld.

Indeed, as con- ﬁrmed by the expected energy levels shown in Fig. 2(b), exciplex host systems are expected to aid in the dissociation of any dark triplets formed within the EML because the weakly bound donor-acceptor charge transfer state in the exciplex host has a lower energy than the host triplet states.

## C. Theory and simulation

To formulate theoretical expectations for exciton lifetime modulations, we solve for the electromagnetic ﬁeld

inside the OLED using dyadic Green’s functions to calculate the coupling strength of bright triplets to surface plasmon polaritons at the organic-cathode interface [16], as shown in Fig. 8. We conﬁrm that modulation of the bright triplet lifetime is independent of other device characteristics through examination of the current-voltage characteristics in Fig. 10. We summarize the modulation by its associated quenching factor QF = τ 0/τ, where τ 0 is the exciton lifetime in vacuum, and τ is the exciton lifetime in the OLED. Integrating the calculated radiative and nonradiative rates over the emission spectrum of PtON-TBBI yields expected quenching factors of QF = 3.1, 2.2, and 1.3 for the fast, medium, and slow devices, respectively. We construct two kinetic models to analyze blue phosphorescent OLED stability and eﬃciency roll-oﬀ: a “minimal” model taking into account only bright triplets and charges, and a “combined” model adding dark exciton interactions. Speciﬁcally, the “combined” model supplements a conventional “minimal” OLED kinetic model by considering interconversion between dark and bright triplets, with rates kD→B and kB→D, as well as interconversion of dark triplets and polarons, with rates kD sep and kD rec. ## III. METHODS

## A. Device fabrication

In-house fabricated and patterned indium tin oxide (ITO) was used as the substrate for OLED growth. The ITO was cleaned by manual scrubbing with detergent for 10 min. Substrates were then sequentially cleaned in two baths of deionized water, two baths of acetone, and two baths of isopropyl alcohol, each for 15 min under ultrasonication. Organic materials were synthesized in-house or provided by Universal Display Corporation. Layer deposition was carried out in a thermal evaporator at highvacuum pressure below 5 × 10−8 Torr. Organic layers were deposited at a rate of 0.3 Å s−1; metal layers were deposited at a rate of 1.4 Å s−1. In-detail documentation

## B. Characterization

OLED current-voltage characterization was carried out using a Keithley source measure unit (SMU), and luminance was detected using a calibrated silicon photodiode. All devices were measured in a nitrogen atmosphere with oxygen and moisture levels below 1 ppm immediately after device fabrication. Degradation measurements were carried out on as-fabricated devices in the same nitrogen environment without any prior current-voltage sweeps. Time-correlated single photon counting (TCSPC) was carried out on a PicoHarp 300 TCSPC module. Sample excitation was carried out at λ = 405 nm with a Pico- Quant LDH-P-C-405 with a less than 90 ps pulse duration. Photon detection used a single-photon avalanche photodiode (MPD PDM Series, 50 μm). The setup’s instrument response function (IRF) was 64 ps. All samples measured with TCSPC in this work were excited at a 125 kHz laser repetition rate and base excitation power of 500 nW. Excitation power was adjusted to keep emission signal constant for all devices of varying cathode reﬂectivity. Reference measurements at half and double the excitation density were taken to ensure obtained triplet exciton lifetimes were excitation-power independent. Triplet exciton lifetimes, τ, were obtained by ﬁtting to a simple monoexponential

decay function of the form PL = a · exp(t/τ), where t is time and a is a constant. For magnetic ﬁeld eﬀect (MFE) measurements, fabricated OLEDs were encapsulated in situ under a nitrogen atmosphere (<1 ppm H2O and O2) using a piece of glass adhered to the substrate with an ultraviolet-cured adhesive OG159-2 purchased from Epoxy Technology Inc. MFE measurements were then carried out in a water-cooled electromagnet model 3470 by GMW Magnet Systems. Samples were placed in a gap of about 1.5 inches (37 mm) between the two magnet poles, yielding a maximum magnetic strength of about 0.4 T. Constant current was applied to devices using a Keithley SMU. Electroluminescence was detected with a silicon photodetector 818-SL by Newport connected to a lock-in ampliﬁer (SR830, Stanford Research Systems) to maximize signal-to-noise ratio.

## B. Magnetic exciton annihilation modulation

To experimentally conﬁrm that the superior performance of exciplex hosts is indeed due to the dissociation of dark excitons, we apply MEAM to electroluminescence from the single-host and exciplex-host OLEDs with identical “fast” cathodes. As discussed above, an applied magnetic ﬁeld of B ∼0.4 T is expected to signiﬁcantly perturb the energy levels of dark triplet states, altering annihilation rates for their collisions with charges and other dark triplets, while bright triplet behavior remains unaﬀected. The MEAM characteristics of the two devices shown in Fig. 5 are notably diﬀerent. First, the single-host device has a much larger signal overall at low ﬁeld, which indicates that there are more species with small zero-ﬁeld splitting interacting with the weak magnetic ﬁeld in the singlehost device. Second, the exciplex host has a monotonic response to the ﬁeld, while the single host initially gets less eﬃcient before becoming brighter at high ﬁeld. The diﬀering shape in single and exciplex MEAM indicates that there are diﬀerent spin-dependent processes that aﬀect electroluminescence in each device. TPA is known to have a monotonic response to magnetic ﬁeld, whereas TTA has a nonmonotonic response, which is consistent with the presence of TTA in the singlehost device and not the exciplex host [20]. Indeed, through ﬁtting the MEAM data we ﬁnd a partial TTA signature involving dark triplets in the single-host devices and zero ﬁeld splitting parameter D = 40–60 μeV as described in Appendix G. The observed dominance of TPA is consistent with previous studies [9–11,25,26]. The positive MEAM trend at high ﬁelds conﬁrms that dark triplets largely undergo energy transfer to bright triplets as expected in the model proposed in Fig. 1(a), i.e., reducing the annihilation of dark triplets under a magnetic ﬁeld increases the electroluminescence from bright triplets.

In contrast, the exciplex host device shows a very weak MEAM signal and no evidence of TTA. We successfully ﬁtted the exciplex host MEAM data with a TPA characteristic deﬁned by D = 3–10 μeV as described in Appendix G. ## V. CONCLUSIONS

Studies of OLED degradation typically consider complex phenomena such as charge balance and its potential impact on triplet annihilation. Subsequent modiﬁcations to materials or the device structure seek to demonstrate improved stability. Unfortunately, even if the device stability is observed to improve, it can be diﬃcult to control for complex changes within OLEDs when the materials or structure is modiﬁed. The advantage of a technique such as SPPM is that it only modulates phenomena that depend on the density of bright triplets, including bimolecular losses such as TPA or TTA. It follows that observing a very weak dependence on the lifetime of bright triplets, as in the single-host devices of Fig. 3(b), provides conclusive evidence that degradation is driven by other, darker states that are unaﬀected by modulations in the lifetime of bright triplets. Phosphorescent molecules within OLEDs are typically expected to quench dark triplets either by energy transfer or by promoting charge transfer and exciplex formation. Blue OLEDs, however, diﬀer from green and red devices because they have notably smaller energetic diﬀerences between guest, host, and blocking layer energy levels, thus reducing the probability of host-to-emitter exciton quenching as well as enhancing emitter-to-host back transfer. Indeed, kinetic model ﬁts and characterization using SPPM and MEAM conﬁrm that dark triplets play a crucial role in the eﬃciency and stability of the studied blue phosphorescent OLEDs. Although dark triplets may be neglected at low bias, where phosphorescent OLEDs approach unity eﬃciency, the impact of dark triplets increases at higher current densities, contributing to eﬃciency roll-oﬀ, instability, and other commonly-cited “charge balance” phenomena. In particular, the eﬃciency roll-oﬀof single-host OLEDs can only be modeled by considering dark triplets. The stability of single-host OLEDs is also dependent on dark triplets, exhibiting a weak dependence on the lifetime of bright triplets that contrasts dramatically with prior optical studies [13]. Crucially, this observation is inconsistent with the conventional model of phosphorescent OLED degradation: instability in the single-host devices is not dominated by interactions between bright triplets and “unbalanced” charges or other triplets. The exciplex host devices, however, ﬁt conventional kinetic models that ignore dark triplets and exhibit a stronger dependence on the lifetime

of the bright excitons. We attribute these results to destabilization of dark triplets in the exciplex host. This, in turn, contributes to improved eﬃciency and stability in exciplex host devices and also enhances the attainable beneﬁts of Purcell engineering—one of the most attractive approaches to realizing stable, high-eﬃciency blue phosphorescent OLEDs. Relative to the conventional “slow” single-host control, the combined beneﬁt of Purcell engineering and reduction of dark triplets provides a ×3.5 improvement in device stability. The dark triplet interpretation of dynamics in single-host blue phosphorescent OLEDs is supported by MEAM measurements that observe the presence of annihilation interactions between dark triplets, conﬁrming that dark triplets are present in densities suﬃcient to support bimolecular annihilation. The density of dark triplets is signiﬁ- cantly reduced by the exciplex host, with a corresponding decrease in the magnetic ﬁeld signature. Indeed, we show here that in-situ magnetic ﬁeld modulation of dark triplet interactions is an especially promising tool for characterizing and controlling dark triplets in the quest for more stable blue phosphorescent OLEDs.

## 5. Modeling conclusions

Using a kinetic scheme that considers polarons, bright triplets, and dark triplets, we deﬁne a “minimal” model that includes only the processes that govern polarons and bright triplets and a “combined” model that adds those of dark triplets as well as interconversion between bright and dark. The PL experimental data for both the single-host and exciplex-host OLEDs are well ﬁtted using a minimal model of charge separation and recombination as well as radiative rates speciﬁc to each coupling layer. Keeping these PL-determined rates ﬁxed, ﬁtting to the roll-oﬀcurves of each device resulted in many well-ﬁtting yet highly ﬂexible and underdetermined models. Some rates are constrained by the experimental data, while others ranged over many orders of magnitude with no eﬀect on the quality of the ﬁt. Despite the high degree of ﬂexibility, however, the single-host roll-oﬀcurves could not be well ﬁtted using any version of the minimal model. Instead, the introduction of dark triplet processes with the combined model was necessary to recreate the correct curve shape. In contrast, the roll-oﬀcurves for the exciplex host devices required only a minimal model and no additional dark triplet rates to achieve a good ﬁt. This remains true even when we consider subsets of the experimental data, as described in Appendix E.IV.
